prompt: Match each event to its outcome.
hint: Second word: what the detector said.

pairs.left: the alert fires on somebody guessing passwords
the alert fires on a backup job with an old password
a slow guesser stays under the rule
a typo followed by a successful login, no alert

prompt: In "false negative", what does the word "negative" refer to?

choices.text: What the detector said: no alert
choices.why: Right. False says the no alert was wrong.

choices.text: A negative score on the matrix
choices.why: The matrix counts cases; nothing is negative.

choices.text: That the attack failed
choices.why: The outcome of the attack is not in the name.

choices.text: That nothing bad happened
choices.why: Something bad did happen; that is why it is false.

prompt: Why is a smoke detector tuned to accept false positives?

choices.text: Insurance requires exactly one alarm per week
choices.why: No such requirement.

choices.text: Smoke is always dangerous
choices.why: Toast smoke is not; the tuning accepts it anyway.

choices.text: A false negative there is a fire
choices.why: Right. Burnt toast costs much less.

choices.text: False positives are impossible to avoid in any device
choices.why: They are avoidable; the tuning is a choice.

prompt: Which costs more, in the lesson's terms: a false positive or a false negative?

choices.text: They always cost the same
choices.why: They cost different things.

choices.text: It depends on the setting
choices.why: Right. Attention against whatever the attack achieves.

choices.text: A false negative, in every situation
choices.why: A spam filter is tuned the other way.

choices.text: A false positive, since it wastes somebody's time
choices.why: One costs minutes; the other can cost what the attack achieves.

prompt: How many sign-in attempts does logins.csv hold, not counting its header line?
Where does the truth the detector is measured against come from?

choices.text: From the detector's own alerts
choices.why: Measuring a detector by itself proves nothing.

choices.text: From the purple exercise's own schedule
choices.why: Right. Its two source addresses.

choices.text: From the CVE list
choices.why: CVEs name software flaws, not events.

choices.text: From whichever accounts failed most
choices.why: The backup failed most and was harmless.

prompt: The detector cuts each time to its first fifteen characters. What does that achieve?

choices.text: One key per ten minutes
choices.why: Right. 14:00:00 to 14:09:59 share one key.

choices.text: It converts the time to the São Paulo time zone
choices.why: Cutting a string converts nothing.

choices.text: It removes the date so weekends count the same
choices.why: The date is kept.

choices.text: It hides the time from the analyst for privacy
choices.why: Privacy is not the reason.

prompt: At threshold 5: TP 3, FP 7. What is the precision, in percent?

choices.text: How many alerts a week does it raise?
choices.why: That is a count, not recall.

choices.text: When it alerts, how often is it right?
choices.why: That is precision.

choices.text: Of the harmless cases, how many did it alert on?
choices.why: That is the false positive rate.

choices.text: Of the real attacks, how many did it catch?
choices.why: Right. TP ÷ (TP + FN).

prompt: At threshold 5, why did every window of the slow guesser end up a false negative?

choices.text: The slow guesser used the office network
choices.why: It came from 203.0.113.77, on the internet.

choices.text: At most three failures per window
choices.why: Right. Under five, so never an alert.

choices.text: Its address was missing from red-team-sources.txt
choices.why: It was listed; that is why the misses count as FN.

choices.text: Its attempts succeeded, so they were not failures
choices.why: They all failed.

prompt: Match each name to the measure it is another name for.
Moving the threshold from 5 to 3 raised recall from 27% to 82%. What happened to the false positives?

choices.text: They disappeared
choices.why: The backup job is still there.

choices.text: They fell, since precision rose
choices.why: Precision rose because true positives grew faster.

choices.text: They rose from seven to twelve
choices.why: Right. Staff with three or four typos now alert too.

choices.text: They stayed at seven
choices.why: Five staff windows were added.

prompt: At threshold 3, how many alerts did the detector raise in the week?
Ignoring svc-backup raised precision to 64% with recall unchanged. What does the lesson say that exception costs?

choices.text: Recall drops on the next exercise
choices.why: The capture showed recall unchanged.

choices.text: The backup job stops working
choices.why: The detector does not touch the job.

choices.text: Silence for guesses at that account
choices.why: Right. Fix the job's credential instead.

choices.text: Nothing; it is a free improvement
choices.why: It is not free.

prompt: Why can no threshold on this rule catch the slow guesser and leave the staff alone?

choices.text: The rule is written in Python
choices.why: The language is irrelevant.

choices.text: The staff use the same address as the guesser
choices.why: The addresses differ.

choices.text: Thresholds must be odd numbers
choices.why: No such rule.

choices.text: Three failures look the same from either
choices.why: Right. The count alone cannot separate them.

prompt: A detector catches 99% of attacks and wrongly alerts on 1% of harmless cases. With 10,000 cases a day and one attack, about what is its precision?

choices.text: About 99%
choices.why: That is its recall, not its precision.

choices.text: About 50%
choices.why: False alerts outnumber true ones a hundred to one.

choices.text: About 10%
choices.why: Work it out: 1 ÷ 101.

choices.text: Around 1%
choices.why: Right. The base rate fallacy.

prompt: How does alert fatigue turn false positives into false negatives?

choices.text: Too many alerts slow the detector until it stops
choices.why: The detector keeps working.

choices.text: Attackers send fake alerts to hide real ones
choices.why: That is not what fatigue means here.

choices.text: The real alert gets closed along with the noise
choices.why: Right. The alert fired; nobody believed it.

choices.text: The detector deletes old alerts to save space
choices.why: It happens in people, not in the detector.

prompt: Which of these does the lesson recommend against alert fatigue? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: grade alerts by how urgent they are
choices.why: A summary for some, a phone for few.

choices.text: count alerts per week, per rule
choices.why: A rule nobody acts on is a finding.

choices.text: fix noisy sources at the cause
choices.why: Like the backup credential.

choices.text: alert on everything, just in case
choices.why: That is how fatigue starts.

prompt: The two-by-two grid of TP, FP, FN and TN is called a ___ matrix.
hint: It shows where the detector mixes things up.
